analysis.one_liner: Creates tax- and regulation-free "Economic Freedom Zones" in bankrupt or poor areas, cutting taxes to 5%, waiving environmental rules, and banning federal city bailouts.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced: it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in December 2013 and died there when the Congress ended, with no committee vote or floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let bankrupt, insolvent, or high-poverty areas apply to become "Economic Freedom Zones" for ten years. Inside a zone, individuals and corporations would pay a flat 5% federal income tax, capital gains would be taxed at zero, payroll taxes would be cut, and the zone would be exempt from major Clean Air Act and Clean Water Act provisions and from Davis-Bacon prevailing wage rules. It would also ban federal bailouts of bankrupt or insolvent cities, offer large K-12 school-choice tax credits, and create investor visas for those putting money into the zones. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Corporations and individual investors who locate in a designated zone would gain most: a 5% flat income tax (with the corporate rate limited to firms under $500 million in adjusted gross income), zero capital gains tax on zone assets and real estate, reduced payroll taxes, and doubled equipment-expensing limits. Wealthier families in the zones would also gain from a $5,000-per-student K-12 school-choice tax credit and up to $40,000 per year in deductible education savings account contributions. City and state governments facing bankruptcy would gain a decade of tax and regulatory relief as an alternative to federal rescue.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Businesses, investors, and school-choice families in zones

how_it_helps.text: Individuals and corporations inside a designated zone would pay a flat 5% federal income tax instead of normal rates, owe no alternative minimum tax, and owe no capital gains tax on zone property and business assets held long enough [S3].
Payroll taxes would drop to 4.2% for workers and employers in the zones, with the lost Social Security revenue repaid from the general fund [S3].

Families in a zone could claim a tax credit of up to $5,000 per year for K-12 tuition at public, private, or religious schools, plus tax-deductible education savings accounts with up to $40,000 in annual contributions [S3].
TitLe VI and Title VII would suspend Davis-Bacon prevailing wage rules in the zones and urge states to adopt right-to-work laws, lower state taxes, pension restructuring, and school choice [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal and state taxpayers would cover the lost revenue, including general-fund transfers to backfill the Social Security trust funds after the payroll tax cut. Workers on zone construction projects could be paid less without Davis-Bacon prevailing wages. Residents of distressed zones would bear relaxed air and water enforcement. If a city goes bankrupt, its employees and pensioners would have no federal assistance to fall back on. Public schools could lose Title I funds as dollars follow children to private schools.
analysis.who_pays_short: General taxpayers, zone workers, and public schools

drawbacks.text: In designated zones, the EPA could not enforce key Clean Air Act and Clean Water Act permitting rules and the Wild and Scenic Rivers Act would not apply, so environmental safeguards would be suspended in the very communities chosen because they are distressed [S2][S3].
Davis-Bacon prevailing wage requirements would not apply in the zones, meaning federally connected construction work there could be done at lower wages than anywhere else [S3].

Individuals and corporations in a zone would pay a 5% flat income tax and zero capital gains tax, a large revenue loss that would be shifted to taxpayers elsewhere, and the payroll tax cut's cost would be repaid from the general fund to keep Social Security trust funds whole [S3].

The bill prohibits federal assistance to states or municipalities in bankruptcy or judged insolvent, which could leave municipal employees, retirees, and bondholders with no federal backstop during a local fiscal collapse [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The stated goal — reviving impoverished places — is real, and school choice credits would put money in families' hands. But the costs are serious: the bill would strip environmental protection in the poorest areas (where pollution is often already worst), cut the wages construction workers must be paid, hand corporations and investors a 5% flat tax and tax-free capital gains, and block any federal help to bankrupt cities whose workers and retirees depend on it. Whether a decade of near-tax-free status would actually create lasting local jobs is unproven; that the benefits flow mostly through business owners and investors is certain.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate and sent to the Finance Committee, which never acted on it, so it expired when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on December 18, 2013, by Senator Rand Paul for himself and Senator Mitch McConnell, read twice, and referred to the Senate Finance Committee [S5][S1].
No further action was ever taken: the Finance Committee held no markup, the bill never reached the Senate floor, and it died at the end of the 113th Congress in January 2015 [S5].

The bill would have barred federal assistance to bankrupt or insolvent states and municipalities, except for areas designated as Economic Freedom Zones, which would instead get a 5% flat income tax, zero capital gains tax, reduced payroll taxes, and exemptions from major environmental rules and Davis-Bacon wage requirements [S2][S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained directly, but the absence of the law left environmental rules, Davis-Bacon wages, and federal support for distressed cities untouched; the tax-free zone plan's prospective beneficiaries never received them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo held; zones' prospective beneficiaries got nothing

for.name: Sen. Rand Paul
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and pushed its design: 5% flat tax, zero capital gains tax, regulatory exemptions, and a federal bailout ban for distressed cities [S1][S3].

for.name: Sen. Mitch McConnell
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor at introduction [S1][S3][S4].

for.name: Senate Finance Committee
for.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never took it up; no markup, no vote, no report [S5].

sides.party_line_note: Both senators attached to the bill were Republicans, and no Democrat cosponsored it [S4]; the bill never advanced far enough for a roll-call.

industries.industry: Businesses and investors locating in designated distressed areas
industries.note: They would pay a 5% flat income tax, zero capital gains tax, reduced payroll taxes, and much larger equipment expensing for ten years [S3]. Their interest runs partly with residents (more jobs) but the tax benefits are designed to reward capital, not wages.

industries.industry: Private and religious schools and education companies
industries.note: A $5,000 federal tax credit per student and funds portable to accredited private schools would channel public money toward private education [S3].
Davis-Bacon prevailing wage rules would not apply in the zones, allowing below-scale pay on federal projects in exactly the areas the bill targets [S3].

industries.industry: Environmental regulation (EPA enforcement and covered water/river protections)
industries.note: The bill exempts the zones from key Clean Air Act and Clean Water Act provisions and the Wild and Scenic Rivers Act, so polluting activity would face fewer constraints in designated areas [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Municipal bond markets and public pension funds
industries.note: A federal bailout ban raises the risk of holding debt from distressed cities, pushing costs onto local workers and retirees; the sense-of-the-Senate section urges states to convert pensions to defined-contribution plans [S3].
